clue.text: United boss works out some words for the media

indicators.note: works out suggests the letters being exercised and rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: The head of a football club called United is thinking up quotes for the press.
explanation.walkthrough: 'works out' signals rearranging UNITED plus BOSS; 'United boss' reads as a football manager, so the solver should not look for a synonym of either word.
explanation.definitionFit: Short quotable snippets supplied to journalists and broadcasters are what the media call these.

clue.text: Something to prod horse? It's just a game

parts.note: a stud is a stallion kept for breeding
a poker is a rod used to prod a fire

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether jabbing a horse with a stick is only a bit of fun.
explanation.walkthrough: STUD POKER is the card game in which some cards are dealt face up.
explanation.definitionFit: A form of poker in which some cards are dealt face up is a card game.

clue.text: Lender has a new taboo

parts.note: uncle is old slang for a pawnbroker, who lends money on goods

explanation.surface: A moneylender has a fresh prohibition to announce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' is a link. Uncle as pawnbroker is old British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unclean is forbidden or ritually impure, which is what a taboo thing is.

clue.text: Kills with a look

definitions.meaning: to butcher is to slaughter or kill brutally
... hook rhymes with look in Cockney rhyming slang, shortened to ...

explanation.walkthrough: Cockney rhyming slang: 'butcher's hook' = look, so 'have a butcher's' means take a look. 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To butcher is to slaughter; a butcher's, from Cockney butcher's hook, is a look.

clue.text: Drug demonstrated brought about reduced temperature

indicators.note: brought about means the protest word is brought around the other letter

parts.note: to sit in is to protest by occupying a place, so demonstrated is sat in
temperature reduced to its abbreviation, T

explanation.surface: A medicine that was shown to lower a fever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'demonstrated' looks like 'showed' but means held a protest: SAT IN. 'brought about' puts T inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A statin is a cholesterol-lowering medicine, so it is a drug.

clue.text: I'm at back of choir — a mistake to ignore leader

indicators.note: ignoring the leader means the first letter of the word for mistake is dropped

parts.note: a lapse is a slip or mistake

explanation.surface: A singer admits to standing at the rear of the choir after a blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to ignore leader' drops the L from LAPSE. The definition speaks in the first person as the part of a church that lies behind the choir; the 'a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: In a church the semicircular recess at the east end lies beyond the choir stalls.

clue.text: Assistant keeps desires close

indicators.note: keeps means the assistant word holds the desires word inside it

parts.note: an aide is an assistant
to long is to desire, so desires are longs

explanation.surface: A helper hides away his yearnings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'close' looks like a verb or 'shut', but here it means near, the adjective sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Alongside means beside or near, a synonym of close in position.

clue.text: In such a triangle, can see line needs adjusting

indicators.note: needs adjusting means the letters must be changed around into a new order

explanation.surface: A geometry pupil is told the line in the triangle diagram is wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'needs adjusting' rearranges CAN SEE plus L. 'In' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A triangle whose three sides all differ in length is the scalene kind.

clue.text: Reveal Sam, say, is about to back horse

indicators.note: about means going round, so the uncle word is placed around the other pieces

parts.note: Uncle Sam is the personification of the USA, so Sam is an example of an uncle

indicators.note: back means the little word to is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
H is slang for heroin, which is called horse

explanation.surface: Someone called Sam is about to put money on a racehorse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back horse' looks like placing a bet, but 'back' is the reversal signal (giving OT) and horse is slang for heroin; 'about' wraps the uncle round them.
explanation.definitionFit: To unclothe something is to strip off its covering, laying it bare or revealing it.

clue.text: Not good wool, beginning to knit garment

indicators.note: Not here tells us to leave out the letter for good from the wool word

parts.note: angora is a soft wool from the angora goat or rabbit

indicators.note: beginning to knit means only the first letter of knit is taken

explanation.surface: A knitter complains that cheap wool is being used to start a new jumper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not good' removes G from ANGORA to give ANORA; 'beginning to knit' adds K.
explanation.definitionFit: A hooded waterproof jacket is a kind of outer garment worn against the weather.

clue.text: Huntsman's strip

to strip the skin off fruit is to pare it

explanation.walkthrough: John Peel was an 18th-19th century fox-hunting man from Cumbria, celebrated in a well-known English folk song.
explanation.definitionFit: John Peel is the huntsman of the old English song, and to strip fruit of its skin is to pare it.

clue.text: Stadium's title: The Field

parts.note: a heading is the title at the top of a page or article
ley, also spelt lea, is an old word for a meadow or field

explanation.surface: A newspaper headline announcing a sports ground's name, as if it were a magazine called The Field.
explanation.walkthrough: HEADINGLEY is a cricket and rugby ground in Leeds, Yorkshire. 'The Field' looks like a title in its own right, the name of a country magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: Headingley in Leeds is a famous cricket and rugby venue, so it is an example of a stadium.

clue.text: Seafood right for two men to eat

parts.note: in chess the king and the pawn are both pieces called men

indicators.note: to eat means the second chessman swallows the letter for right

parts.note: the second chessman is the pawn

explanation.surface: A dish of seafood is suitable for a couple of diners.
explanation.walkthrough: Chess pieces are often called men, so 'two men' supplies both of the chessmen; 'to eat' means the second swallows R.
explanation.definitionFit: A large edible crustacean, often served as a starter, is a kind of seafood.

clue.text: Looking angry in middle of night, and scowling

indicators.note: middle of takes the centre letter of the five-letter word night

parts.note: to lower, rhyming with flower, is to frown or scowl

explanation.surface: Someone in the small hours glares and frowns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'middle of' gives G from NIGHT. Lower, pronounced to rhyme with flower, means to frown.
explanation.definitionFit: To glower is to stare angrily, so glowering means looking angry.

clue.text: Right to keep stocking new underwear

indicators.note: stocking here means holding in stock, so the right contains the letter for new

parts.note: a lien is a legal right to keep someone's property until a debt is paid

explanation.surface: A shopper insists on the right to have new underwear and hosiery in stock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stocking' looks like hosiery but signals containment: LIEN holds N. 'Right to keep' is one phrase defining LIEN, a lawyer's term.
explanation.definitionFit: Body linen is an old term for undergarments and shirts, once mostly made of that cloth.

clue.text: US agent and wife? Not married — he's absorbed in himself

indicators.note: Not means the letter for married is left out of the wife word

parts.note: missus is informal for a wife

explanation.walkthrough: 'Not married' removes M from MISSUS to give ISSUS. Narcissus of Greek myth fell in love with his own reflection.
explanation.definitionFit: In myth the youth who fell for his own reflection, hence a byword for a self-absorbed man.

clue.text: Script calls for taller Greek

explanation.definitionFit: Hieratic is the cursive script used by ancient Egyptian priests, a simplified hieroglyphic writing.

clue.text: Cheer, installing British machine

parts.note: to root for a team is to cheer for it

explanation.walkthrough: 'installing' puts B inside ROOT.

clue.text: Ring, as it happens, fitted with popular stone

clue.text: This is in cockpit, for when captain wants his feet up
